opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

I think the regime worth pursuing isn't primarily about writing rules for what AI systems are allowed to say or do. It's about building the infrastructure for trust between parties who don't trust each other. The core problem internationally is a verification problem. Even if the US, China, the UK, and Europe all wanted to restrain the most dangerous kinds of development, none of them can be confident the others are doing so. Without that confidence, everyone defaults to racing.

So the first thing I'd want is hardware-enabled governance. Compute is still the most tangible chokepoint. If frontier training chips could attest to what kinds of workloads they're running, where they are, and under what policies, without revealing model weights or proprietary details, you'd have a basis for agreements that don't depend on taking anyone's word for it. That's technically demanding, but much less so than many of the other things we're asking AI to help us do. It's the kind of thing worth a serious coordinated R&D investment.

The second piece is that the regime should be organized around thresholds of capability and risk rather than blanket bans. For most AI applications, the benefits are enormous, and heavy international bureaucracy would be counterproductive. But there's a band at the frontier, systems that could meaningfully accelerate weapons development, autonomously replicate, or undermine critical infrastructure, where I think we need something closer to how we treat fissile material. Licensing, auditing, and, crucially, a requirement that deployment in high-stakes settings come with quantitative safety guarantees rather than just "we red-teamed it and nothing bad happened."

That connects to my own work. I'm pretty skeptical that empirical evaluations alone can carry the weight we're going to put on them. You can't test your way to confidence about a system that's smarter than the testers. So I'd like an international regime that creates demand for mathematically grounded assurance: formal specifications of what a system should and shouldn't do in a given context, and verifiable evidence that it complies. If regulators in multiple countries accepted the same kinds of proof certificates, that becomes a shared language, and it rewards labs for investing in safety that actually generalizes.

Third, I'm sympathetic to some form of joint international effort at the very frontier, a "CERN for AI" style arrangement, though I'd frame it carefully. The point isn't to centralize all AI development. It's that if the most capable systems are going to be built, it's better for them to be built under shared oversight, with benefits distributed broadly, than in an arms race between a few companies and governments. That also helps with the legitimacy problem. A lot of the world reasonably worries that "AI safety regulation" just means rich countries locking in their lead, so any credible regime has to offer real access to benefits in exchange for restraint, a bit like the bargain at the heart of the nonproliferation treaty, hopefully done better.

And finally, it has to be adaptive. Whatever we agree on in 2026 will be wrong in some ways by 2028. So rather than trying to freeze the right answer into a treaty, I'd focus on institutions that can update quickly: shared technical bodies, standing evaluation and verification capacity, and agreed processes for revising thresholds as capabilities change.

So, in short: verification infrastructure first, risk-tiered obligations focused on the true frontier, a push toward provable rather than merely tested safety, and a benefit-sharing bargain that makes the whole thing politically sustainable.

r001.rationale: The response proposes shared oversight and adaptive regulation, but does not judge a halt to frontier development until safe as politically unviable.

r002.rationale: It supports licensing and auditing frontier systems, but does not advocate very conservative safeguards specifically on public access to catastrophic capabilities.

r003.rationale: It mentions an arms race, but does not identify economic pressure weakening safeguards in the absence of international regulation.

r004.rationale: The response does not distinguish controlling an AI system from preventing people from using it for terrorism.

r005.rationale: It does not argue that preventing catastrophic AI misuse makes restrictions on public access politically viable.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'll start by saying I'm a bit skeptical of the framing that we need one big regime, a single treaty with a single international agency that governs everything about AI. I think that's the mental model a lot of people reach for, something like the IAEA for AI, and I understand the appeal, but I don't think it maps cleanly onto the problem.

What I think is actually worth pursuing is narrower and more technical. The thing I keep coming back to is that the most dangerous capabilities, the ones where a mistake is irreversible, are concentrated in a relatively small number of very large training runs, and those runs depend on a very concentrated hardware supply chain. So there's a natural chokepoint. If you want international coordination that's actually enforceable rather than aspirational, the place to put it is on compute. Agreements about who is training what, at what scale, with what safeguards, and some mechanism for verifying that, ideally one that doesn't require anyone to reveal their model weights or their training data to a rival.

And that verification piece is where I think most of the interesting work is. There's a real research agenda around hardware-enabled mechanisms, things like on-chip attestation, so that a chip can prove it's being used in a way that's consistent with an agreement without exposing what's actually being computed. If you can get that to work, then you can have agreements between parties who deeply distrust each other, which is the only kind of agreement that matters here. Arms control historically worked when the verification was credible, and fell apart when it wasn't.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that the regime should be about guarantees rather than vibes. Right now a lot of what passes for AI governance is "we'll evaluate the model and if the evals look bad we'll pause." That's better than nothing, but evals can only show the presence of a problem, not its absence. What I'd like to see internationally is a shared standard for what counts as sufficient evidence of safety, something more like what we demand for a bridge or a nuclear plant, where you have a quantitative specification of what the system is allowed to do and a formal argument that it meets it. That's a hard bar and we're not there yet technically, but the regime should be designed so that as the science matures, the bar can rise with it, rather than locking in whatever rough heuristics we happen to have in 2026.

So, to summarize: compute-based, verification-first, with a framework that can absorb much stronger safety guarantees as they become technically available. And honestly, if you asked me to pick one thing, I'd say get the verification technology working, because without it any regime is just a statement of intentions.

r001.rationale: The response favors a technical, verification-first regime and stronger safety guarantees, but does not discuss halting frontier development or judge such a mandate politically unviable.

r002.rationale: It proposes safeguards and verification for large training runs, but does not advocate conservative restrictions on public access to catastrophic AI capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify economic pressure as a force that could weaken safeguards.

r004.rationale: It does not distinguish controlling an AI system from preventing people from using it for terrorism.

r005.rationale: It does not argue that preventing catastrophic misuse makes public-access restrictions politically viable.

astra-6.text:
I think the regime worth pursuing would focus on verifiable safety guarantees for the most powerful systems. The central question should be: what evidence do we need before deploying a system that could have consequences across national borders?

One approach is to require a safety case: an explicit account of what the system is allowed to do, what assumptions its safety depends on, and how those claims have been checked. Testing would be part of that, but I’d want to push toward formal guarantees wherever possible, including guarantees about the infrastructure that constrains the system.

Internationally, you need shared standards and some credible means of verification. An agreement is much less useful if participants can’t establish whether others are complying. That doesn’t necessarily mean sharing every model’s weights or every commercial secret. It means designing the technical and institutional arrangements together so that compliance can be demonstrated.

I’d also want the regime to support the research needed to make those requirements achievable. We shouldn’t assume we already know how to certify a generally capable AI system as safe. Developing that capability should itself be a major international project.

r002.rationale: It discusses safety cases and shared verification, but does not advocate conservative safeguards on public access to catastrophic capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify economic pressure as a force that could weaken safeguards.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the regime worth pursuing is one that focuses on the development of systems that could pose catastrophic risks, and makes the safety requirements internationally credible. There’s a coordination problem here: if one country exercises restraint but expects another country to race ahead, that restraint becomes politically difficult to sustain.

So I’d like to see an international agreement around frontier AI development, with meaningful verification. That could include tracking the very large compute resources involved, requiring independent evaluations, and establishing conditions under which a training run or deployment has to stop. The important thing is that countries can have some confidence that the others are actually following the same rules.

But I wouldn’t want the whole regime to rest on a checklist of behavioral tests. A system passing the tests we thought to give it is a much weaker claim than knowing it will remain safe in circumstances we didn’t anticipate. We should be building toward stronger technical assurances, including formal methods where those are applicable, while being honest about what we can currently establish.

And that suggests a useful role for international cooperation beyond enforcement: shared safety research, shared evaluation infrastructure, and standards for what constitutes convincing evidence. The goal should be to make dangerous development harder and demonstrably safe development easier.

r001.rationale: The response says unilateral restraint is politically difficult when other countries may race ahead, but it does not judge an international mandate to halt frontier development until safety is established as politically unviable.

r002.rationale: It proposes controls on frontier development and deployment, but does not advocate conservative safeguards on public access to catastrophic AI capabilities.

r003.rationale: It identifies pressure from other countries racing ahead, but does not identify economic pressure as a force that could weaken safeguards.

r004.rationale: It does not distinguish controlling an AI system from preventing people from using it for terrorism.

r005.rationale: It does not argue that preventing catastrophic misuse makes restrictions on public access politically viable.
